chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shummun from Muhammad ibn Isa from Safwan from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Umar ibn Hanzalah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about two men from our companions who have a dispute regarding a debt or inheritance, and they refer themselves to the Sultan or to the judges; is that permissible?

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever refers to the Taghut (imperial/judicial authority) and he rules for him, then he is taking a bribe/unjustly, even if his right is established, because he took by the rule of the Taghut, and Allah (Exalted and Mighty) commanded that it be disbelieved in.'
He said: 'Look among you to the one who has narrated our hadith and examined our halal and haram and knows our rulings; let them accept him as a judge, for I have made him a ruler over you.'

'So when he rules with our ruling and it is not accepted from him, then by the rule of Allah it was slighted, and to us it was returned, and the one who returns to us is the one who returns to Allah, and he is on the verge of shirk with Allah (Exalted and Mighty).'

key_terms.حَدِيثُنَا: Our hadith (the narration of the Imam)
key_terms.حَلاَلِنَا وَ حَرَامِنَا: Our halal and haram (permissible and forbidden rulings)

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on referring to secular courts or judges for resolving disputes between Muslims?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the foundational principle of 'Nass al-Faqih' (designation of the jurist), where Imam al-Sadiq explicitly appoints the learned jurist as his deputy in judicial matters, thereby legitimizing early Shia legal authority independent of the Abbasid state. The Imam warns that rejecting the jurist's ruling is equivalent to rejecting the Imam himself, and by extension, rejecting God, elevating the jurist's authority to a level of divine representation. This narrative serves as a primary textual evidence for the development of the Marja'iyyah system in Shia jurisprudence.
